# omq_compio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/omq-compio/0.12.6/omq_compio/

## Expand description

omq-compio - compio-runtime backend for omq.

Built on compio’s thread-per-core executor with io_uring (Linux),
IOCP (Windows), and kqueue (macOS) drivers. Each `Socket`
is pinned to the executor it was created on; cross-executor sends
use a runtime-agnostic mpsc (flume).

The codec, message types, mechanism handshakes, and routing
algorithms come from the runtime-agnostic `omq-proto` crate.
This crate provides only the runtime glue.

Supports all ZMTP socket types, TCP/IPC/inproc/UDP/WebSocket transports, CURVE/BLAKE3ZMQ/PLAIN mechanisms, and lz4 compression.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use monitor::`- [MonitorStream](https://docs.rs/monitor/struct.MonitorStream.html);
- `pub use runtime::`- [DEFAULT_BUFFER_POOL_COUNT](https://docs.rs/runtime/constant.DEFAULT_BUFFER_POOL_COUNT.html);
- `pub use runtime::`- [DEFAULT_BUFFER_POOL_LEN](https://docs.rs/runtime/constant.DEFAULT_BUFFER_POOL_LEN.html);
- `pub use runtime::`- [ProactorBuilderExt](https://docs.rs/runtime/trait.ProactorBuilderExt.html);
- `pub use runtime::`- [build_default_runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/fn.build_default_runtime.html);
- `pub use socket::`- [Socket](https://docs.rs/socket/struct.Socket.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/index.html)
- Endpoint parsing and formatting.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error and Result types.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Message, Frame, and Payload types.
- [monitor](https://docs.rs/monitor/index.html)
- Monitor: socket-like consumer of connection-lifecycle events.
- [options](https://docs.rs/options/index.html)
- Socket options: typed builder.
- [proto](https://docs.rs/proto/index.html)
- Sans-I/O ZMTP 3.x codec.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Runtime-builder helpers for sizing compio’s `BUF_RING`buffer pool.
- [socket](https://docs.rs/socket/index.html)
- Socket actor for omq-compio.
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- Transport implementations for omq-compio.

# camel_component_llm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-component-llm/0.22.0/camel_component_llm/

## Expand description

camel-component-llm — LLM integration component for rust-camel.

Provides chat (streaming + materialized), embeddings, tool calling, and multi-turn conversations through multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Ollama, Mock). Features include response caching with single-flight, cost observability (config-driven pricing tables), retry with per-attempt delay override (ADR-0021), and concurrency control via producer semaphore.

Uses a project-owned `LlmProvider` trait with strict adapter boundary
isolating the siumai SDK to exactly two production files (ADR-0020).

# tt-call 1.0.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tt-call/1.0.9

# Token Tree Calling Convention

**This library is an attempt at seeding an ecosystem of high-quality modular
interoperable tt-muncher building blocks.**

Tt-munching is a powerful technique for parsing macro_rules input grammars of significant complexity. In building more and more sophisticated tt-muncher macros it becomes valuable to share code for dealing with certain common input patterns, rather than reimplementing support for those patterns in a low quality and poorly tested way each time.

The core macros provided by this library are

`tt_call!`**. Together these provide a flexible way to propagate input and output tokens along a recursive descent call hierarchy. One may also view them as a flexible library-only stable implementation of eager expansion for macro_rules.**

`tt_return!````
[]
 = "1.0"
```
*Version requirement: tt-call requires a Rust compiler version 1.31 or
newer.*

## Calling convention rules

-
**Macros that conform to tt-call must be invoked with curly braces.**`some_macro!`The Rust grammar is very particular about punctuation after parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations. In expression or type position they must not be followed by a semicolon. In item or statement position they are required to be followed by a semicolon. The inconsistency is applied transitively to any helper macros they forward to, and means that parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations must decide whether to support expression and type position only or item and statement position only. They cannot support both, which is a problem for broadly applicable macro building blocks. There is no such punctuation requirement after curly brace invocations. Consistently using curly braces makes the same macro building blocks usable in any syntactic position.
-
**Input and output values must be passed in the following key-value form.**`$key:ident =`This is enforced by the `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`macros. The consistency is important for composability and makes it possible to write higher-order macros that operate on the input or output of an arbitrary tt-call macro.Except in libraries intended specifically as tt-call building blocks, generally tt-call macros will be private `#[doc(hidden)]`helpers with a user-facing non-tt-call entry point. Thus the rigid key-value syntax need not be exposed to users of the public macro.
-
**Before its key-value inputs, every rule must accept a**`$caller:tt`.This is an opaque tt bundle used by `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`to record the call hierarchy. A`tt_return!`accepts a`$caller`to return back to.
-
**Every rule must expand to exactly one macro invocation and nothing else.**Output tokens are expected to be returned through `tt_return!`. Expanding to nothing, expanding to more than one macro invocation, or expanding to anything other than a macro invocation are not permitted.

## Examples

Just as a flavor of the syntax, one of the rules from the implementation of
the built-in [ tt_replace!](https://docs.rs/tt-call/1.0/tt_call/macro.tt_replace.html) macro is written as follows. The macro takes in
a token stream and for each token that matches a given predicate it replaces
that token with a given replacement sequence of tokens. For example the
caller may want to replace the token

`self` with the single token `__value`.The rule shown here is responsible for performing one step of the
replacement. It matches one token of input in `$first:tt`, uses [ tt_if!](https://docs.rs/tt-call/1.0/tt_call/macro.tt_if.html)
to invoke the predicate with

`$first` as input, recurses with an accumulated
copy of the replacement tokens if the predicate returns true, and recurses
on the remaining tokens with `$first` preserved unchanged if the predicate
returns false.```
 => ;
```
Here is another macro rule selected from `tt_replace!`. This one matches if
the tt-muncher has reached the end of its input. It returns the finished
tokens back to the caller using `tt_return!`.

```
 => ;
```
One example of a caller-provided predicate for `tt_replace!` could be
written as follows. This predicate determines whether the input token is
lowercase `self`.

```
]
    } => ;
    // Input token is anything other than `self`.
     => ;
}
```
From here, calling `tt_replace!` with our `is_lowercase_self!` as the
condition predicate can be used to implement a fanciful syntax for unary
closures: `closure!(self + 1)` should expand to `|__value| __value + 1`.

Notice that this user-facing `closure!` macro does not follow the tt-call
calling convention. Internally though it uses several tt-call helpers as
building blocks.

```
```
## Motivation

This may seem like a lot of ceremony around what should be very simple macro
calls. After all, couldn't we write `is_lowercase_self` in a much more
straightforward way as follows?

```
```
Qualified yes. As written, the simpler `is_lowercase_self!` behaves as it
looks like it should.

But suppose we want to build `tt_replace!` or similar macro that needs to
invoke `is_lowercase_self!` as a helper. There is no way to do it with this
simpler one. No matter what our macro does, there is no way for it to expand
`is_lowercase_self!` before expanding itself. If it expands itself first,
there is no way for it to use the expansion of `is_lowercase_self!` to
decide whether the current token is supposed to be replaced.

The `tt_call!` and `tt_return!` abstraction along with `$caller:tt` tracking
of the call hierarchy are critical to building composable macros that freely
pass around arbitrary tokens and return in a way that can inform expansion
of their caller.

A future eager expansion feature for declarative macros may render the
tt-call approach unnecessary. Eager expansion is listed as an unresolved
question in the [tracking issue for declarative macros 2.0](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/39412) but is
believed to be quite a ways out, if it ever happens. And even then it is not
clear whether it is desirable to allow macros expanding to arbitrary tokens.
Today macros always expand to an expression, item, statement, type, or
pattern. Eager expansion does not automatically mean that the restriction
would be lifted to allow a macro that expands to arbitrary tokens such as `! @ #`. The token tree calling convention provides working eager expansion
today with support for passing and returning arbitrary token streams.

And function-like procedural macros once those are stable? It is going to depend on your choice of syntax for the macro input whether a procedural macro is a better choice, but note that they present their own DIY parsing adventures and can be even nastier than tt-call once you get the hang of both. In addition, procedural macros must be defined in a separate crate from the rest of your library so they are not well suited for quick one-off helper macros.

## Design philosphy

As may be no surprise by this point, the calling convention design prioritizes scalability and composability over conciseness. A reader familiar with the calling convention (maybe you, six months after writing the macro) should be able to look at any individual tt-call rule by itself and comfortably read off what it does top to bottom and identify its purpose.

## Links

-
The code that implements `closure!(self + 1)`, all of which is shown above, can be found all together in`examples/replace.rs`
-
As a more elaborate example of a tt-call macro, `examples/comma_separated.rs``parse_type!``$:ty`.`static MANGLED: & = mangle_type_names!`

# tt_call - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tt-call/1.0.9/target-redirect/tt_call/

## Expand description

**This library is an attempt at seeding an ecosystem of high-quality modular
interoperable tt-muncher building blocks.**

Tt-munching is a powerful technique for parsing macro_rules input grammars of significant complexity. In building more and more sophisticated tt-muncher macros it becomes valuable to share code for dealing with certain common input patterns, rather than reimplementing support for those patterns in a low quality and poorly tested way each time.

The core macros provided by this library are

`tt_call!`**. Together these provide a flexible way to propagate input and output tokens along a recursive descent call hierarchy. One may also view them as a flexible library-only stable implementation of eager expansion for macro_rules.**

`tt_return!````
[dependencies]
tt-call = "1.0"
```
*Version requirement: tt-call requires a Rust compiler version 1.31 or
newer.*

[§](https://docs.rs#calling-convention-rules)Calling convention rules

-
**Macros that conform to tt-call must be invoked with curly braces.**`some_macro! { /* ... */ }`The Rust grammar is very particular about punctuation after parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations. In expression or type position they must not be followed by a semicolon. In item or statement position they are required to be followed by a semicolon. The inconsistency is applied transitively to any helper macros they forward to, and means that parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations must decide whether to support expression and type position only or item and statement position only. They cannot support both, which is a problem for broadly applicable macro building blocks. There is no such punctuation requirement after curly brace invocations. Consistently using curly braces makes the same macro building blocks usable in any syntactic position.
-
**Input and output values must be passed in the following key-value form.**`$key:ident = [{ $($value:tt)* }]`This is enforced by the `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`macros. The consistency is important for composability and makes it possible to write higher-order macros that operate on the input or output of an arbitrary tt-call macro.Except in libraries intended specifically as tt-call building blocks, generally tt-call macros will be private `#[doc(hidden)]`helpers with a user-facing non-tt-call entry point. Thus the rigid key-value syntax need not be exposed to users of the public macro.
-
**Before its key-value inputs, every rule must accept a**`$caller:tt`.This is an opaque tt bundle used by `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`to record the call hierarchy. A`tt_return!`accepts a`$caller`to return back to.
-
**Every rule must expand to exactly one macro invocation and nothing else.**Output tokens are expected to be returned through `tt_return!`. Expanding to nothing, expanding to more than one macro invocation, or expanding to anything other than a macro invocation are not permitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Just as a flavor of the syntax, one of the rules from the implementation of
the built-in [ tt_replace!](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_replace.html) macro is written as follows. The macro takes in
a token stream and for each token that matches a given predicate it replaces
that token with a given replacement sequence of tokens. For example the
caller may want to replace the token

`self` with the single token `__value`.The rule shown here is responsible for performing one step of the
replacement. It matches one token of input in `$first:tt`, uses [ tt_if!](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_if.html)
to invoke the predicate with

`$first` as input, recurses with an accumulated
copy of the replacement tokens if the predicate returns true, and recurses
on the remaining tokens with `$first` preserved unchanged if the predicate
returns false.```
{
    $caller:tt
    condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
    replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
    tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
    rest = [{ $first:tt $($rest:tt)* }]
} => {
    tt_if! {
        condition = [{ $condition }]
        input = [{ $first }]
        true = [{
            private_replace! {
                $caller
                condition = [{ $condition }]
                replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
                tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $($with)* }]
                rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
            }
        }]
        false = [{
            private_replace! {
                $caller
                condition = [{ $condition }]
                replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
                tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $first }]
                rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
            }
        }]
    }
};
```
Here is another macro rule selected from `tt_replace!`. This one matches if
the tt-muncher has reached the end of its input. It returns the finished
tokens back to the caller using `tt_return!`.

```
{
    $caller:tt
    condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
    replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
    tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
    rest = [{ }]
} => {
    tt_return! {
        $caller
        tokens = [{ $($tokens)* }]
    }
};
```
One example of a caller-provided predicate for `tt_replace!` could be
written as follows. This predicate determines whether the input token is
lowercase `self`.

```
macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
    // Input token is `self`.
    {
        $caller:tt
        input = [{ self }]
    } => {
        tt_return! {
            $caller
            is = [{ true }]
        }
    };
    // Input token is anything other than `self`.
    {
        $caller:tt
        input = [{ $other:tt }]
    } => {
        tt_return! {
            $caller
            is = [{ false }]
        }
    };
}
```
From here, calling `tt_replace!` with our `is_lowercase_self!` as the
condition predicate can be used to implement a fanciful syntax for unary
closures: `closure!(self + 1)` should expand to `|__value| __value + 1`.

Notice that this user-facing `closure!` macro does not follow the tt-call
calling convention. Internally though it uses several tt-call helpers as
building blocks.

```
macro_rules! closure {
    ($($expr:tt)+) => {
        |__value| tt_call! {
            macro = [{ tt_replace }]
            condition = [{ is_lowercase_self }]
            replace_with = [{ __value }]
            input = [{ $($expr)+ }]
        }
    };
}
fn main() {
    let add_one = closure!(self + 1);
    println!("{}", add_one(1));
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

This may seem like a lot of ceremony around what should be very simple macro
calls. After all, couldn’t we write `is_lowercase_self` in a much more
straightforward way as follows?

```
macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
    (self) => { true };
    ($other:tt) => { false };
}
fn main() {
    println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(self)); // true
    println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(not_self)); // false
}
```
Qualified yes. As written, the simpler `is_lowercase_self!` behaves as it
looks like it should.

But suppose we want to build `tt_replace!` or similar macro that needs to
invoke `is_lowercase_self!` as a helper. There is no way to do it with this
simpler one. No matter what our macro does, there is no way for it to expand
`is_lowercase_self!` before expanding itself. If it expands itself first,
there is no way for it to use the expansion of `is_lowercase_self!` to
decide whether the current token is supposed to be replaced.

of the call hierarchy are critical to building composable macros that freely
pass around arbitrary tokens and return in a way that can inform expansion
of their caller.

tt-call approach unnecessary. Eager expansion is listed as an unresolved
question in the [tracking issue for declarative macros 2.0](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/39412) but is
believed to be quite a ways out, if it ever happens. And even then it is not
clear whether it is desirable to allow macros expanding to arbitrary tokens.
Today macros always expand to an expression, item, statement, type, or
pattern. Eager expansion does not automatically mean that the restriction
would be lifted to allow a macro that expands to arbitrary tokens such as `! @ #`. The token tree calling convention provides working eager expansion
today with support for passing and returning arbitrary token streams.

It is going to depend on your choice of syntax for the macro input whether a procedural macro is a better choice, but note that they present their own DIY parsing adventures and can be even nastier than tt-call once you get the hang of both. In addition, procedural macros must be defined in a separate crate from the rest of your library so they are not well suited for quick one-off helper macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-philosphy)Design philosphy

[§](https://docs.rs#links)Links

-

-
As a more elaborate example of a tt-call macro, `examples/comma_separated.rs``parse_type!``$:ty`.`static MANGLED: &[&str] = mangle_type_names! { std::fs::File, &'a mut str, impl Display, fn(s: &str) -> String, }; fn main() { assert_eq!(MANGLED, [ "_std_fs_File", "_ref_mut_str", "_impl_Display", "_fn_s_ref_str_to_String", ]); }`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [error_](https://docs.rs/macro.error_eof.html)- eof
- Fail due to an unexpected end of input.
- [error_](https://docs.rs/macro.error_unexpected.html)- unexpected
- Fail due to an unexpected input token.
- [error_](https://docs.rs/macro.error_unexpected_last.html)- unexpected_ - last
- Fail due to an unexpected input token, faulting the last token.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_type.html)- type
- Parse any syntactically valid Rust type.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_call](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_call.html)
- Evaluate a tt-call macro and return its output to a given return destination.
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_debug.html)- debug
- Print arbitrary output values returned by a tt-call macro. This is valuable
for debugging.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_false.html)- false
- Predicate that is always false.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_if](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_if.html)
- Evaluate a condition and expand to one or the other of two branches.
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_is_comma.html)- is_ - comma
- Predicate that accepts a single token and determines whether it is a comma.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_is_ident.html)- is_ - ident
- Predicate that accepts a single token and determines whether it is an
identifier.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_is_lifetime.html)- is_ - lifetime
- Predicate that accepts a single token and determines whether it is a
lifetime token.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_replace.html)- replace
- Replace each token that matches a given predicate by a given replacement
sequence of tokens.
**[tt-call]**
- [tt_](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_return.html)- return
- Return zero or more output values to the caller macro.
- [tt_true](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_true.html)
- Predicate that is always true.
**[tt-call]**

# tt_call - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tt-call/1.0.9/tt_call/index.html

## Expand description

**This library is an attempt at seeding an ecosystem of high-quality modular
interoperable tt-muncher building blocks.**

Tt-munching is a powerful technique for parsing macro_rules input grammars of significant complexity. In building more and more sophisticated tt-muncher macros it becomes valuable to share code for dealing with certain common input patterns, rather than reimplementing support for those patterns in a low quality and poorly tested way each time.

The core macros provided by this library are

`tt_call!`**. Together these provide a flexible way to propagate input and output tokens along a recursive descent call hierarchy. One may also view them as a flexible library-only stable implementation of eager expansion for macro_rules.**

`tt_return!````
[dependencies]
tt-call = "1.0"
```
*Version requirement: tt-call requires a Rust compiler version 1.31 or
newer.*

[§](https://docs.rs#calling-convention-rules)Calling convention rules

-
**Macros that conform to tt-call must be invoked with curly braces.**`some_macro! { /* ... */ }`The Rust grammar is very particular about punctuation after parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations. In expression or type position they must not be followed by a semicolon. In item or statement position they are required to be followed by a semicolon. The inconsistency is applied transitively to any helper macros they forward to, and means that parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations must decide whether to support expression and type position only or item and statement position only. They cannot support both, which is a problem for broadly applicable macro building blocks. There is no such punctuation requirement after curly brace invocations. Consistently using curly braces makes the same macro building blocks usable in any syntactic position.
-
**Input and output values must be passed in the following key-value form.**`$key:ident = [{ $($value:tt)* }]`This is enforced by the `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`macros. The consistency is important for composability and makes it possible to write higher-order macros that operate on the input or output of an arbitrary tt-call macro.Except in libraries intended specifically as tt-call building blocks, generally tt-call macros will be private `#[doc(hidden)]`helpers with a user-facing non-tt-call entry point. Thus the rigid key-value syntax need not be exposed to users of the public macro.
-
**Before its key-value inputs, every rule must accept a**`$caller:tt`.This is an opaque tt bundle used by `tt_call!`and`tt_return!`to record the call hierarchy. A`tt_return!`accepts a`$caller`to return back to.
-
**Every rule must expand to exactly one macro invocation and nothing else.**Output tokens are expected to be returned through `tt_return!`. Expanding to nothing, expanding to more than one macro invocation, or expanding to anything other than a macro invocation are not permitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Just as a flavor of the syntax, one of the rules from the implementation of
the built-in [ tt_replace!](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_replace.html) macro is written as follows. The macro takes in
a token stream and for each token that matches a given predicate it replaces
that token with a given replacement sequence of tokens. For example the
caller may want to replace the token

`self` with the single token `__value`.The rule shown here is responsible for performing one step of the
replacement. It matches one token of input in `$first:tt`, uses [ tt_if!](https://docs.rs/macro.tt_if.html)
to invoke the predicate with

`$first` as input, recurses with an accumulated
copy of the replacement tokens if the predicate returns true, and recurses
on the remaining tokens with `$first` preserved unchanged if the predicate
returns false.```
{
    $caller:tt
    condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
    replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
    tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
    rest = [{ $first:tt $($rest:tt)* }]
} => {
    tt_if! {
        condition = [{ $condition }]
        input = [{ $first }]
        true = [{
            private_replace! {
                $caller
                condition = [{ $condition }]
                replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
                tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $($with)* }]
                rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
            }
        }]
        false = [{
            private_replace! {
                $caller
                condition = [{ $condition }]
                replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
                tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $first }]
                rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
            }
        }]
    }
};
```
Here is another macro rule selected from `tt_replace!`. This one matches if
the tt-muncher has reached the end of its input. It returns the finished
tokens back to the caller using `tt_return!`.

```
{
    $caller:tt
    condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
    replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
    tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
    rest = [{ }]
} => {
    tt_return! {
        $caller
        tokens = [{ $($tokens)* }]
    }
};
```
One example of a caller-provided predicate for `tt_replace!` could be
written as follows. This predicate determines whether the input token is
lowercase `self`.

```
macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
    // Input token is `self`.
    {
        $caller:tt
        input = [{ self }]
    } => {
        tt_return! {
            $caller
            is = [{ true }]
        }
    };
    // Input token is anything other than `self`.
    {
        $caller:tt
        input = [{ $other:tt }]
    } => {
        tt_return! {
            $caller
            is = [{ false }]
        }
    };
}
```
From here, calling `tt_replace!` with our `is_lowercase_self!` as the
condition predicate can be used to implement a fanciful syntax for unary
closures: `closure!(self + 1)` should expand to `|__value| __value + 1`.

Notice that this user-facing `closure!` macro does not follow the tt-call
calling convention. Internally though it uses several tt-call helpers as
building blocks.

```
macro_rules! closure {
    ($($expr:tt)+) => {
        |__value| tt_call! {
            macro = [{ tt_replace }]
            condition = [{ is_lowercase_self }]
            replace_with = [{ __value }]
            input = [{ $($expr)+ }]
        }
    };
}
fn main() {
    let add_one = closure!(self + 1);
    println!("{}", add_one(1));
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

This may seem like a lot of ceremony around what should be very simple macro
calls. After all, couldn’t we write `is_lowercase_self` in a much more
straightforward way as follows?

```
macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
    (self) => { true };
    ($other:tt) => { false };
}
fn main() {
    println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(self)); // true
    println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(not_self)); // false
}
```
Qualified yes. As written, the simpler `is_lowercase_self!` behaves as it
looks like it should.

But suppose we want to build `tt_replace!` or similar macro that needs to
invoke `is_lowercase_self!` as a helper. There is no way to do it with this
simpler one. No matter what our macro does, there is no way for it to expand
`is_lowercase_self!` before expanding itself. If it expands itself first,
there is no way for it to use the expansion of `is_lowercase_self!` to
decide whether the current token is supposed to be replaced.

The `tt_call!` and `tt_return!` abstraction along with `$caller:tt` tracking
of the call hierarchy are critical to building composable macros that freely
pass around arbitrary tokens and return in a way that can inform expansion
of their caller.

A future eager expansion feature for declarative macros may render the
tt-call approach unnecessary. Eager expansion is listed as an unresolved
question in the [tracking issue for declarative macros 2.0](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/39412) but is
believed to be quite a ways out, if it ever happens. And even then it is not
clear whether it is desirable to allow macros expanding to arbitrary tokens.
Today macros always expand to an expression, item, statement, type, or
pattern. Eager expansion does not automatically mean that the restriction
would be lifted to allow a macro that expands to arbitrary tokens such as `! @ #`. The token tree calling convention provides working eager expansion
today with support for passing and returning arbitrary token streams.

And function-like procedural macros once those are stable? It is going to depend on your choice of syntax for the macro input whether a procedural macro is a better choice, but note that they present their own DIY parsing adventures and can be even nastier than tt-call once you get the hang of both. In addition, procedural macros must be defined in a separate crate from the rest of your library so they are not well suited for quick one-off helper macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-philosphy)Design philosphy

As may be no surprise by this point, the calling convention design prioritizes scalability and composability over conciseness. A reader familiar with the calling convention (maybe you, six months after writing the macro) should be able to look at any individual tt-call rule by itself and comfortably read off what it does top to bottom and identify its purpose.

[§](https://docs.rs#links)Links

-
The code that implements `closure!(self + 1)`, all of which is shown above, can be found all together in`examples/replace.rs`
-
As a more elaborate example of a tt-call macro, `examples/comma_separated.rs``parse_type!``$:ty`.`static MANGLED: &[&str] = mangle_type_names! { std::fs::File, &'a mut str, impl Display, fn(s: &str) -> String, }; fn main() { assert_eq!(MANGLED, [ "_std_fs_File", "_ref_mut_str", "_impl_Display", "_fn_s_ref_str_to_String", ]); }`

[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! **This library is an attempt at seeding an ecosystem of high-quality modular
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! interoperable tt-muncher building blocks.**
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!

[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! of significant complexity. In building more and more sophisticated
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! tt-muncher macros it becomes valuable to share code for dealing with certain
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! common input patterns, rather than reimplementing support for those patterns
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! in a low quality and poorly tested way each time.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! The core macros provided by this library are **[`tt_call!`]** and
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! **[`tt_return!`]**. Together these provide a flexible way to propagate input
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! and output tokens along a recursive descent call hierarchy. One may also
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! view them as a flexible library-only stable implementation of eager
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! expansion for macro\_rules.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! [`tt_call!`]: macro.tt_call.html
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [`tt_return!`]: macro.tt_return.html
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! ```toml
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [dependencies]
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! tt-call = "1.0"
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! ```
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! *Version requirement: tt-call requires a Rust compiler version 1.31 or
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! newer.*
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! ## Calling convention rules
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! - **Macros that conform to tt-call must be invoked with curly braces.**
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!     ```
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     # macro_rules! some_macro {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     #     () => {};
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     # }
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     #
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     some_macro! {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!         /* ... */
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     }
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!     ```
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     The Rust grammar is very particular about punctuation after
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations. In expression or
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!     type position they must not be followed by a semicolon. In item or
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     statement position they are required to be followed by a semicolon. The
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     inconsistency is applied transitively to any helper macros they forward
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     to, and means that parenthesized and square bracketed macro invocations
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     must decide whether to support expression and type position only or item
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!     and statement position only. They cannot support both, which is a
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     problem for broadly applicable macro building blocks.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     There is no such punctuation requirement after curly brace invocations.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     Consistently using curly braces makes the same macro building blocks
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     usable in any syntactic position.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! - **Input and output values must be passed in the following key-value
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!   form.**
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     # macro_rules! some_macro {
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     #     {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!     $key:ident = [{ $($value:tt)* }]
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     #     } => {};
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!     # }
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     ```
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     This is enforced by the `tt_call!` and `tt_return!` macros. The
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     consistency is important for composability and makes it possible to
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     write higher-order macros that operate on the input or output of an
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     arbitrary tt-call macro.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     Except in libraries intended specifically as tt-call building blocks,
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     generally tt-call macros will be private `#[doc(hidden)]` helpers with a
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!     user-facing non-tt-call entry point. Thus the rigid key-value syntax
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     need not be exposed to users of the public macro.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! - **Before its key-value inputs, every rule must accept a `$caller:tt`.**
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     This is an opaque tt bundle used by `tt_call!` and `tt_return!` to
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!     record the call hierarchy. A `tt_return!` accepts a `$caller` to return
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     back to.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! - **Every rule must expand to exactly one macro invocation and nothing
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!   else.**
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!     Output tokens are expected to be returned through `tt_return!`.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!     Expanding to nothing, expanding to more than one macro invocation, or
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!     expanding to anything other than a macro invocation are not permitted.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! ## Examples
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! Just as a flavor of the syntax, one of the rules from the implementation of
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! the built-in [`tt_replace!`] macro is written as follows. The macro takes in
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! a token stream and for each token that matches a given predicate it replaces
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! that token with a given replacement sequence of tokens. For example the
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! caller may want to replace the token `self` with the single token `__value`.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! The rule shown here is responsible for performing one step of the
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! replacement. It matches one token of input in `$first:tt`, uses [`tt_if!`]
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! to invoke the predicate with `$first` as input, recurses with an accumulated
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! copy of the replacement tokens if the predicate returns true, and recurses
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! on the remaining tokens with `$first` preserved unchanged if the predicate
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! returns false.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! [`tt_replace!`]: macro.tt_replace.html
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! [`tt_if!`]: macro.tt_if.html
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! ```
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! # macro_rules! ignore {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     $caller:tt
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!     condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!     tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!     rest = [{ $first:tt $($rest:tt)* }]
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! } => {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!     tt_if! {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!         condition = [{ $condition }]
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!         input = [{ $first }]
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!         true = [{
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!             private_replace! {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!                 $caller
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!                 condition = [{ $condition }]
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!                 replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!                 tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $($with)* }]
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!                 rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!             }
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!         }]
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!         false = [{
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!             private_replace! {
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!                 $caller
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!                 condition = [{ $condition }]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!                 replace_with = [{ $($with)* }]
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!                 tokens = [{ $($tokens)* $first }]
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!                 rest = [{ $($rest)* }]
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!             }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!         }]
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     }
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! };
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! # }
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! ```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! Here is another macro rule selected from `tt_replace!`. This one matches if
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! the tt-muncher has reached the end of its input. It returns the finished
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! tokens back to the caller using `tt_return!`.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! # macro_rules! ignore {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     $caller:tt
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     condition = [{ $condition:ident }]
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!     replace_with = [{ $($with:tt)* }]
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     tokens = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     rest = [{ }]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! } => {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     tt_return! {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!         $caller
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!         tokens = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     }
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! };
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! # }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! ```
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! One example of a caller-provided predicate for `tt_replace!` could be
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! written as follows. This predicate determines whether the input token is
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! lowercase `self`.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! ```
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!     // Input token is `self`.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!     {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!         $caller:tt
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!         input = [{ self }]
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!     } => {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!         tt_return! {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!             $caller
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!             is = [{ true }]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!         }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     };
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!     // Input token is anything other than `self`.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!         $caller:tt
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!         input = [{ $other:tt }]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!     } => {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!         tt_return! {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!             $caller
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!             is = [{ false }]
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!         }
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!     };
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! ```
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! From here, calling `tt_replace!` with our `is_lowercase_self!` as the
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! condition predicate can be used to implement a fanciful syntax for unary
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! closures: `closure!(self + 1)` should expand to `|__value| __value + 1`.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! Notice that this user-facing `closure!` macro does not follow the tt-call
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! calling convention. Internally though it uses several tt-call helpers as
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! building blocks.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! ```
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! # macro_rules! tt_call {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! #     ($($ignore:tt)*) => {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! #         2
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! #     };
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! # }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! #
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! macro_rules! closure {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!     ($($expr:tt)+) => {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!         |__value| tt_call! {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!             macro = [{ tt_replace }]
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!             condition = [{ is_lowercase_self }]
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!             replace_with = [{ __value }]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!             input = [{ $($expr)+ }]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!         }
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!     };
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! fn main() {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!     let add_one = closure!(self + 1);
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!     println!("{}", add_one(1));
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! ```
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! ## Motivation
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! This may seem like a lot of ceremony around what should be very simple macro
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! calls. After all, couldn't we write `is_lowercase_self` in a much more
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! straightforward way as follows?
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! ```
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!     (self) => { true };
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!     ($other:tt) => { false };
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! }
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! fn main() {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!     println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(self)); // true
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!     println!("{}", is_lowercase_self!(not_self)); // false
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! ```
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! Qualified yes. As written, the simpler `is_lowercase_self!` behaves as it
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! looks like it should.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! But suppose we want to build `tt_replace!` or similar macro that needs to
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! invoke `is_lowercase_self!` as a helper. There is no way to do it with this
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! simpler one. No matter what our macro does, there is no way for it to expand
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! `is_lowercase_self!` before expanding itself. If it expands itself first,
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! there is no way for it to use the expansion of `is_lowercase_self!` to
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! decide whether the current token is supposed to be replaced.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! The `tt_call!` and `tt_return!` abstraction along with `$caller:tt` tracking
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! of the call hierarchy are critical to building composable macros that freely
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! pass around arbitrary tokens and return in a way that can inform expansion
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! of their caller.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! A future eager expansion feature for declarative macros may render the
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! tt-call approach unnecessary. Eager expansion is listed as an unresolved
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! question in the [tracking issue for declarative macros 2.0][tracking] but is
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! believed to be quite a ways out, if it ever happens. And even then it is not
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! clear whether it is desirable to allow macros expanding to arbitrary tokens.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! Today macros always expand to an expression, item, statement, type, or
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! pattern. Eager expansion does not automatically mean that the restriction
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! would be lifted to allow a macro that expands to arbitrary tokens such as `!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! @ #`. The token tree calling convention provides working eager expansion
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! today with support for passing and returning arbitrary token streams.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! [tracking]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/39412
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! And function-like procedural macros once those are stable? It is going to
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! depend on your choice of syntax for the macro input whether a procedural
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! macro is a better choice, but note that they present their own DIY parsing
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! adventures and can be even nastier than tt-call once you get the hang of
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! both. In addition, procedural macros must be defined in a separate crate
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! from the rest of your library so they are not well suited for quick one-off
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! helper macros.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! ## Design philosphy
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! As may be no surprise by this point, the calling convention design
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! prioritizes scalability and composability over conciseness. A reader
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! familiar with the calling convention (maybe you, six months after writing
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! the macro) should be able to look at any individual tt-call rule by itself
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! and comfortably read off what it does top to bottom and identify its
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! purpose.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! ## Links
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! - The code that implements `closure!(self + 1)`, all of which is shown
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!   above, can be found all together in [`examples/replace.rs`].
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! - As a more elaborate example of a tt-call macro,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!   [`examples/comma_separated.rs`] demonstrates a macro that does primitive
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!   name mangling of Rust types. It uses [`parse_type!`] which is a tt-call
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!   version of `$:ty`.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!     ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!     # macro_rules! mangle_type_names {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!     #     ($($ignore:tt)*) => {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!     #         &[
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!     #             "_std_fs_File",
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!     #             "_ref_mut_str",
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!     #             "_impl_Display",
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!     #             "_fn_s_ref_str_to_String",
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!     #         ]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!     #     };
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!     # }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!     #
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!     static MANGLED: &[&str] = mangle_type_names! {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!         std::fs::File,
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!         &'a mut str,
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!         impl Display,
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!         fn(s: &str) -> String,
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!     };
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!     fn main() {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!         assert_eq!(MANGLED, [
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!             "_std_fs_File",
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!             "_ref_mut_str",
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!             "_impl_Display",
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!             "_fn_s_ref_str_to_String",
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!         ]);
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!     }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!     ```
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//!
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! [`examples/replace.rs`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/tt-call/blob/master/examples/replace.rs
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! [`examples/comma_separated.rs`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/tt-call/blob/master/examples/comma_separated.rs
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! [`parse_type!`]: macro.parse_type.html
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)#![no_std]
[345](https://docs.rs#345)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/tt-call/1.0.9")]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)#![allow(clippy::module_name_repetitions, clippy::needless_doctest_main)]
[347](https://docs.rs#347)
[348](https://docs.rs#348)mod predicate;
[349](https://docs.rs#349)mod replace;
[350](https://docs.rs#350)mod rust;
[351](https://docs.rs#351)mod unexpected;
[352](https://docs.rs#352)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)// In general it is not possible today in Rust to produce good error messages
[354](https://docs.rs#354)// and good error spans at the same time. See:
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//     https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44535
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//
[358](https://docs.rs#358)// Within this crate we prefer to produce errors with the right span, even if
[359](https://docs.rs#359)// the message is not good. This scales much better to large input token
[360](https://docs.rs#360)// streams.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// Evaluate a tt-call macro and return its output to a given return
[363](https://docs.rs#363)/// destination.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)///
[365](https://docs.rs#365)/// # Input
[366](https://docs.rs#366)///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)/// The input must start with an argument called `macro` which provides the name
[368](https://docs.rs#368)/// of the macro for `tt_call!` to invoke.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)///
[370](https://docs.rs#370)///   - `macro = [{` name of macro to call `}]`
[371](https://docs.rs#371)///
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// After that there may be any number of key-value pairs to be passed as
[373](https://docs.rs#373)/// arguments to the macro being called.
[374](https://docs.rs#374)///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)///   - **`$(`**<br>
[376](https://docs.rs#376)///       arbitrary key `= [{` arbitrary tokens `}]`<br>
[377](https://docs.rs#377)///     **`)*`**
[378](https://docs.rs#378)///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)/// Finally a specification of the macro invocation to which this call should
[380](https://docs.rs#380)/// return its output.
[381](https://docs.rs#381)///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)///   - `~~>` name of return destination macro `! {`<br>
[383](https://docs.rs#383)///       arbitrary tokens<br>
[384](https://docs.rs#384)///     `}`
[385](https://docs.rs#385)///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// # Examples
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// ```
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// use tt_call::{tt_call, tt_is_ident};
[390](https://docs.rs#390)///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)/// macro_rules! print_is_ident {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)///     {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)///         token = [{ $token:tt }]
[394](https://docs.rs#394)///         is_ident = [{ true }]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)///     } => {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)///         println!("turns out `{}` is an ident", stringify!($token));
[397](https://docs.rs#397)///     };
[398](https://docs.rs#398)///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)///     {
[400](https://docs.rs#400)///         token = [{ $token:tt }]
[401](https://docs.rs#401)///         is_ident = [{ false }]
[402](https://docs.rs#402)///     } => {
[403](https://docs.rs#403)///         println!("nope, `{}` is not an ident", stringify!($token));
[404](https://docs.rs#404)///     };
[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// }
[406](https://docs.rs#406)///
[407](https://docs.rs#407)/// fn main() {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)///     tt_call! {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)///         macro = [{ tt_is_ident }]
[410](https://docs.rs#410)///         input = [{ foo }]
[411](https://docs.rs#411)///         ~~> print_is_ident! {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)///             token = [{ foo }]
[413](https://docs.rs#413)///         }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)///     }
[415](https://docs.rs#415)/// }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)/// ```
[417](https://docs.rs#417)///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)/// If the invoked macro provides the entirety of the input to the return
[419](https://docs.rs#419)/// destination macro, then the `!` and argument list may be omitted.
[420](https://docs.rs#420)///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)/// ```
[422](https://docs.rs#422)/// use tt_call::{tt_call, tt_is_ident};
[423](https://docs.rs#423)///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// macro_rules! print_is_ident {
[425](https://docs.rs#425)///     {
[426](https://docs.rs#426)///         is_ident = [{ true }]
[427](https://docs.rs#427)///     } => {
[428](https://docs.rs#428)///         println!("that token is an ident");
[429](https://docs.rs#429)///     };
[430](https://docs.rs#430)///
[431](https://docs.rs#431)///     {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)///         is_ident = [{ false }]
[433](https://docs.rs#433)///     } => {
[434](https://docs.rs#434)///         println!("nope, not an ident");
[435](https://docs.rs#435)///     };
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// }
[437](https://docs.rs#437)///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)/// fn main() {
[439](https://docs.rs#439)///     tt_call! {
[440](https://docs.rs#440)///         macro = [{ tt_is_ident }]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)///         input = [{ foo }]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)///         ~~> print_is_ident
[443](https://docs.rs#443)///     }
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)/// ```
[446](https://docs.rs#446)///
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// And if the invoked macro produces exactly one output value and we just want
[448](https://docs.rs#448)/// to expand to that output value, the destination macro may be omitted
[449](https://docs.rs#449)/// entirely.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)/// ```
[452](https://docs.rs#452)/// use tt_call::{tt_call, tt_is_ident};
[453](https://docs.rs#453)///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)/// fn main() {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)///     let is_ident = tt_call! {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)///         macro = [{ tt_is_ident }]
[457](https://docs.rs#457)///         input = [{ foo }]
[458](https://docs.rs#458)///     };
[459](https://docs.rs#459)///     println!("{}", is_ident); // prints true or false
[460](https://docs.rs#460)/// }
[461](https://docs.rs#461)/// ```
[462](https://docs.rs#462)#[macro_export]
[463](https://docs.rs#463)macro_rules! tt_call {
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    // Call macro and expand into the tokens of its one return value.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        macro = [{ $($m:ident)::* }]
[467](https://docs.rs#467)        $(
[468](https://docs.rs#468)            $input:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        )*
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    } => {
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        $($m)::* ! {
[472](https://docs.rs#472)            (__tt_call_private $crate::tt_identity_return! {})
[473](https://docs.rs#473)            $(
[474](https://docs.rs#474)                $input = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[475](https://docs.rs#475)            )*
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    };
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    // Call macro and pass its return values to the given return destination.
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    {
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        macro = [{ $($m:ident)::* }]
[482](https://docs.rs#482)        $(
[483](https://docs.rs#483)            $input:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        )*
[485](https://docs.rs#485)        ~~> $($return:ident)::*
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    } => {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)        $($m)::* ! {
[488](https://docs.rs#488)            (__tt_call_private $($return)::* ! {})
[489](https://docs.rs#489)            $(
[490](https://docs.rs#490)                $input = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[491](https://docs.rs#491)            )*
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        }
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    };
[494](https://docs.rs#494)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    // Call macro and append its return values onto the invocation of the given
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    // return destination without caller.
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    {
[498](https://docs.rs#498)        macro = [{ $($m:ident)::* }]
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        $(
[500](https://docs.rs#500)            $input:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[501](https://docs.rs#501)        )*
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        ~~> $($return:ident)::* ! {
[503](https://docs.rs#503)            $(
[504](https://docs.rs#504)                $name:ident = [{ $($state:tt)* }]
[505](https://docs.rs#505)            )*
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        }
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    } => {
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        $($m)::* ! {
[509](https://docs.rs#509)            (__tt_call_private $($return)::* ! {
[510](https://docs.rs#510)                $(
[511](https://docs.rs#511)                    $name = [{ $($state)* }]
[512](https://docs.rs#512)                )*
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            })
[514](https://docs.rs#514)            $(
[515](https://docs.rs#515)                $input = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[516](https://docs.rs#516)            )*
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        }
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    };
[519](https://docs.rs#519)
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    // Call macro and append its return values onto the invocation of the given
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    // return destination with caller.
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    {
[523](https://docs.rs#523)        macro = [{ $($m:ident)::* }]
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        $(
[525](https://docs.rs#525)            $input:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[526](https://docs.rs#526)        )*
[527](https://docs.rs#527)        ~~> $($return:ident)::* ! {
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            $caller:tt
[529](https://docs.rs#529)            $(
[530](https://docs.rs#530)                $name:ident = [{ $($state:tt)* }]
[531](https://docs.rs#531)            )*
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        }
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    } => {
[534](https://docs.rs#534)        $($m)::* ! {
[535](https://docs.rs#535)            (__tt_call_private $($return)::* ! {
[536](https://docs.rs#536)                $caller
[537](https://docs.rs#537)                $(
[538](https://docs.rs#538)                    $name = [{ $($state)* }]
[539](https://docs.rs#539)                )*
[540](https://docs.rs#540)            })
[541](https://docs.rs#541)            $(
[542](https://docs.rs#542)                $input = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[543](https://docs.rs#543)            )*
[544](https://docs.rs#544)        }
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    };
[546](https://docs.rs#546)}
[547](https://docs.rs#547)
[548](https://docs.rs#548)#[doc(hidden)]
[549](https://docs.rs#549)#[macro_export]
[550](https://docs.rs#550)macro_rules! tt_identity_return {
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    // Macro returned one value.
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    {
[553](https://docs.rs#553)        $name:ident = [{ $($output:tt)* }]
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    } => {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)        $($output)*
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    };
[557](https://docs.rs#557)
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    // Macro parsed the entire input and returned one value.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    {
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        $name:ident = [{ $($output:tt)* }]
[561](https://docs.rs#561)        rest = [{ }]
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    } => {
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        $($output)*
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    };
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    // Unexpected: macro failed to parse the entire input.
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)        $name:ident = [{ $($output:tt)* }]
[569](https://docs.rs#569)        rest = [{ $($unexpected:tt)* }]
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    } => {
[571](https://docs.rs#571)        $crate::error_unexpected! {
[572](https://docs.rs#572)            $($unexpected)*
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    };
[575](https://docs.rs#575)}
[576](https://docs.rs#576)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)/// Return zero or more output values to the caller macro.
[578](https://docs.rs#578)///
[579](https://docs.rs#579)/// # Input
[580](https://docs.rs#580)///
[581](https://docs.rs#581)/// The `tt_return!` invocation should be given a `$caller` to return to and a
[582](https://docs.rs#582)/// sequence of zero or more named return values.
[583](https://docs.rs#583)///
[584](https://docs.rs#584)///   - **`$(`**<br>
[585](https://docs.rs#585)///       arbitrary key `= [{` arbitrary tokens `}]`<br>
[586](https://docs.rs#586)///     **`)*`**
[587](https://docs.rs#587)///
[588](https://docs.rs#588)/// # Example
[589](https://docs.rs#589)///
[590](https://docs.rs#590)/// ```
[591](https://docs.rs#591)/// use tt_call::{tt_call, tt_return};
[592](https://docs.rs#592)///
[593](https://docs.rs#593)/// macro_rules! is_lowercase_self {
[594](https://docs.rs#594)///     // Input token is `self`.
[595](https://docs.rs#595)///     {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)///         $caller:tt
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///         input = [{ self }]
[598](https://docs.rs#598)///     } => {
[599](https://docs.rs#599)///         tt_return! {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)///             $caller
[601](https://docs.rs#601)///             is = [{ true }]
[602](https://docs.rs#602)///         }
[603](https://docs.rs#603)///     };
[604](https://docs.rs#604)///
[605](https://docs.rs#605)///     // Input token is anything other than `self`.
[606](https://docs.rs#606)///     {
[607](https://docs.rs#607)///         $caller:tt
[608](https://docs.rs#608)///         input = [{ $other:tt }]
[609](https://docs.rs#609)///     } => {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)///         tt_return! {
[611](https://docs.rs#611)///             $caller
[612](https://docs.rs#612)///             is = [{ false }]
[613](https://docs.rs#613)///         }
[614](https://docs.rs#614)///     };
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// }
[616](https://docs.rs#616)///
[617](https://docs.rs#617)/// fn main() {
[618](https://docs.rs#618)///     let is = tt_call! {
[619](https://docs.rs#619)///         macro = [{ is_lowercase_self }]
[620](https://docs.rs#620)///         input = [{ self }]
[621](https://docs.rs#621)///     };
[622](https://docs.rs#622)///     println!("{}", is);
[623](https://docs.rs#623)/// }
[624](https://docs.rs#624)/// ```
[625](https://docs.rs#625)#[macro_export]
[626](https://docs.rs#626)macro_rules! tt_return {
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)        $caller:tt
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        $(
[630](https://docs.rs#630)            $output:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[631](https://docs.rs#631)        )*
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    } => {
[633](https://docs.rs#633)        $crate::private_return! {
[634](https://docs.rs#634)            $caller
[635](https://docs.rs#635)            $(
[636](https://docs.rs#636)                $output = [{ $($tokens)* }]
[637](https://docs.rs#637)            )*
[638](https://docs.rs#638)        }
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    };
[640](https://docs.rs#640)}
[641](https://docs.rs#641)
[642](https://docs.rs#642)#[doc(hidden)]
[643](https://docs.rs#643)#[macro_export]
[644](https://docs.rs#644)macro_rules! private_return {
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    {
[646](https://docs.rs#646)        (__tt_call_private $($caller:ident)::* ! { $($state:tt)* })
[647](https://docs.rs#647)        $($append:tt)*
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    } => {
[649](https://docs.rs#649)        $($caller)::* ! {
[650](https://docs.rs#650)            $($state)*
[651](https://docs.rs#651)            $($append)*
[652](https://docs.rs#652)        }
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    };
[654](https://docs.rs#654)}
[655](https://docs.rs#655)
[656](https://docs.rs#656)/// Evaluate a condition and expand to one or the other of two branches.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)/// # Input
[659](https://docs.rs#659)///
[660](https://docs.rs#660)///   - `condition = [{` name of predicate macro to invoke `}]`
[661](https://docs.rs#661)///   - `input = [{` arbitrary tokens to pass as input to the predicate `}]`
[662](https://docs.rs#662)///   - `true = [{` tokens to expand to if the predicate returns true `}]`
[663](https://docs.rs#663)///   - `false = [{` and if the predicate returns false `}]`
[664](https://docs.rs#664)///
[665](https://docs.rs#665)/// The predicate macro must accept a single input value named `input`. It is
[666](https://docs.rs#666)/// expected to return a single output value which may have any name but must
[667](https://docs.rs#667)/// hold the tokens `true` or `false`. For example the built-in `tt_is_comma!`
[668](https://docs.rs#668)/// predicate expands to `is_comma = [{ true }]` or `is_comma = [{ false }]`.
[669](https://docs.rs#669)///
[670](https://docs.rs#670)/// # Example
[671](https://docs.rs#671)///
[672](https://docs.rs#672)/// ```
[673](https://docs.rs#673)/// use tt_call::{tt_call, tt_if, tt_is_comma, tt_return};
[674](https://docs.rs#674)///
[675](https://docs.rs#675)/// macro_rules! parse_until_comma {
[676](https://docs.rs#676)///     ($($input:tt)*) => {
[677](https://docs.rs#677)///         tt_call! {
[678](https://docs.rs#678)///             macro = [{ parse_until_comma_helper }]
[679](https://docs.rs#679)///             before_comma = [{ }]
[680](https://docs.rs#680)///             tokens = [{ $($input)* }]
[681](https://docs.rs#681)///         }
[682](https://docs.rs#682)///     };
[683](https://docs.rs#683)/// }
[684](https://docs.rs#684)///
[685](https://docs.rs#685)/// macro_rules! parse_until_comma_helper {
[686](https://docs.rs#686)///     {
[687](https://docs.rs#687)///         $caller:tt
[688](https://docs.rs#688)///         before_comma = [{ $($before:tt)* }]
[689](https://docs.rs#689)///         tokens = [{ $first:tt $($rest:tt)* }]
[690](https://docs.rs#690)///     } => {
[691](https://docs.rs#691)///         tt_if! {
[692](https://docs.rs#692)///             condition = [{ tt_is_comma }]
[693](https://docs.rs#693)///             input = [{ $first }]
[694](https://docs.rs#694)///             true = [{
[695](https://docs.rs#695)///                 tt_return! {
[696](https://docs.rs#696)///                     $caller
[697](https://docs.rs#697)///                     before_comma = [{ $($before)* }]
[698](https://docs.rs#698)///                 }
[699](https://docs.rs#699)///             }]
[700](https://docs.rs#700)///             false = [{
[701](https://docs.rs#701)///                 parse_until_comma_helper! {
[702](https://docs.rs#702)///                     $caller
[703](https://docs.rs#703)///                     before_comma = [{ $($before)* $first }]
[704](https://docs.rs#704)///                     tokens = [{ $($rest)* }]
[705](https://docs.rs#705)///                 }
[706](https://docs.rs#706)///             }]
[707](https://docs.rs#707)///         }
[708](https://docs.rs#708)///     };
[709](https://docs.rs#709)/// }
[710](https://docs.rs#710)///
[711](https://docs.rs#711)/// fn main() {
[712](https://docs.rs#712)///     assert_eq!(3, parse_until_comma!(1 + 2, three, four));
[713](https://docs.rs#713)/// }
[714](https://docs.rs#714)/// ```
[715](https://docs.rs#715)#[macro_export]
[716](https://docs.rs#716)macro_rules! tt_if {
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    {
[718](https://docs.rs#718)        condition = [{ $($condition:ident)::* }]
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        input = [{ $($input:tt)* }]
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        true = [{ $($then:tt)* }]
[721](https://docs.rs#721)        false = [{ $($else:tt)* }]
[722](https://docs.rs#722)    } => {
[723](https://docs.rs#723)        $crate::tt_call! {
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            macro = [{ $($condition)::* }]
[725](https://docs.rs#725)            input = [{ $($input)* }]
[726](https://docs.rs#726)            ~~> $crate::private_if_branch! {
[727](https://docs.rs#727)                true = [{ $($then)* }]
[728](https://docs.rs#728)                false = [{ $($else)* }]
[729](https://docs.rs#729)            }
[730](https://docs.rs#730)        }
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    };
[732](https://docs.rs#732)}
[733](https://docs.rs#733)
[734](https://docs.rs#734)#[doc(hidden)]
[735](https://docs.rs#735)#[macro_export]
[736](https://docs.rs#736)macro_rules! private_if_branch {
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    // Branch condition returned true.
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    {
[739](https://docs.rs#739)        true = [{ $($then:tt)* }]
[740](https://docs.rs#740)        false = [{ $($else:tt)* }]
[741](https://docs.rs#741)        $condition:ident = [{ true }]
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    } => {
[743](https://docs.rs#743)        $($then)*
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    };
[745](https://docs.rs#745)
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    // Branch condition returned false.
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    {
[748](https://docs.rs#748)        true = [{ $($then:tt)* }]
[749](https://docs.rs#749)        false = [{ $($else:tt)* }]
[750](https://docs.rs#750)        $condition:ident = [{ false }]
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    } => {
[752](https://docs.rs#752)        $($else)*
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    };
[754](https://docs.rs#754)}
[755](https://docs.rs#755)
[756](https://docs.rs#756)/// Print arbitrary output values returned by a tt-call macro. This is valuable
[757](https://docs.rs#757)/// for debugging.
[758](https://docs.rs#758)/// <sup>**[tt-call]**</sup>
[759](https://docs.rs#759)///
[760](https://docs.rs#760)/// # Example
[761](https://docs.rs#761)///
[762](https://docs.rs#762)/// ```
[763](https://docs.rs#763)/// use tt_call::{parse_type, tt_call, tt_debug};
[764](https://docs.rs#764)///
[765](https://docs.rs#765)/// fn main() {
[766](https://docs.rs#766)///     tt_call! {
[767](https://docs.rs#767)///         macro = [{ parse_type }]
[768](https://docs.rs#768)///         input = [{ Vec<u8>, compressed=false }]
[769](https://docs.rs#769)///         ~~> tt_debug
[770](https://docs.rs#770)///     }
[771](https://docs.rs#771)/// }
[772](https://docs.rs#772)/// ```
[773](https://docs.rs#773)///
[774](https://docs.rs#774)/// The output is:
[775](https://docs.rs#775)///
[776](https://docs.rs#776)/// ```text
[777](https://docs.rs#777)/// type = [{ Vec < u8 > }]
[778](https://docs.rs#778)/// rest = [{ , compressed = false }]
[779](https://docs.rs#779)/// ```
[780](https://docs.rs#780)#[macro_export]
[781](https://docs.rs#781)macro_rules! tt_debug {
[782](https://docs.rs#782)    {
[783](https://docs.rs#783)        $(
[784](https://docs.rs#784)            $output:ident = [{ $($tokens:tt)* }]
[785](https://docs.rs#785)        )*
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    } => {
[787](https://docs.rs#787)        $(
[788](https://docs.rs#788)            println!(
[789](https://docs.rs#789)                "{}",
[790](https://docs.rs#790)                concat!(
[791](https://docs.rs#791)                    stringify!($output),
[792](https://docs.rs#792)                    " = [{ ",
[793](https://docs.rs#793)                    stringify!($($tokens)*),
[794](https://docs.rs#794)                    " }]",
[795](https://docs.rs#795)                )
[796](https://docs.rs#796)            );
[797](https://docs.rs#797)        )*
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    }
[799](https://docs.rs#799)}
